act1.label: I · The spirit of the house

s02.label: 13 · A Century of Exchange
s02.q1: “In 1927, Geneva opened the doors of its craft to Lange.
s02.q2: A hundred years later, Lange opens the doors of its own to Geneva.”
s02.traceAlt: Two lines leave Geneva and Glashütte in 1927, cross, and arrive on the other side in 2027.

s03.label: 14 · A house that opens its doors
s03.p1: Since 2021, Lange has received its Geneva clients by appointment in its Salon on Place de Longemalle. On Rue Robert-Céard, the house settles on three floors, with its own watchmaker's workshop.
s03.p2: During the opening days, the boutique opens to five audiences. Each discovers the story of 1927 and experiences an encounter between Glashütte and Geneva.
s03.salonCaption: The Salon, Place de Longemalle · A. Lange & Söhne
s03.salonAlt: The Geneva Salon on Place de Longemalle: display cases, appointment table and leather armchairs.
s03.frontAlt: Dark shopfront on Rue Robert-Céard, Geneva, with the street sign.

s04.label: 15 · An encounter at every moment
s04.intro: Every moment of the opening brings Glashütte and Geneva together around a watch, a gesture or a table.
items: A watchmaker from the manufacture and a Geneva watchmaker bent over the same 1927 watch.
An archive from Geneva and an archive from Glashütte in the same display case.
A Geneva chef and a Saxon chef at the stove of the same dinner.
A craftsman from the city and a craftsman from the house for the same gift.
s04.coda: The two cities meet there like old friends, as equals.

s05.label: 16 · The whole story, for every guest
s05.p: Journalists, collectors, prospects, clients and friends of the house do not come at the same time. Yet each receives the whole story: the 1927 story in front of an archive piece, an encounter between the two cities, the discovery of the boutique and the collections, a gift to take home.

s06.label: 17 · The boutique tells the story
s06.p: The boutique has just been designed; nothing in it is moved. The story settles into what it already offers: the history wall and the space devoted to Glashütte on the ground floor, the cinema and the multisensory room on the first floor, the workshop and the private salon on the second.

s07.label: 18 · Two to three days in Geneva
s07.d1: The first day opens with the press, the CEO's address and the ribbon cutting. The afternoon belongs to the collectors.
s07.d2: The next day, clients and prospects discover the boutique in small groups, from morning to evening.
s07.e: Every evening, the boutique closes on a dinner of a few covers for the house's closest friends.
s07.d3: A third day can extend the visits and host one last dinner.

s08.label: 19 · The Exchange of Stories
s08.p1: The press discovers the story through its proof. On the ground floor, a display case shows the branch's entry in the Geneva commercial register, held at the State Archives, beside its publication in the Swiss Official Gazette of Commerce of 6 May 1927.
s08.p2: The CEO speaks, then cuts the ribbon. The journalists then tour the boutique in small groups, up to the workshop where the watchmaker awaits them.
s08.caption: Feuille officielle suisse du commerce, no. 105, 6 May 1927, p. 833 · e-periodica.ch
s08.alt: Full page of the Swiss Official Gazette of Commerce of 6 May 1927, carrying the registration of the Geneva branch of A. Lange & Söhne.

s09.label: 20 · The Exchange of Knowledge
s09.p1: Two watchmakers, one watch from 1927. A watchmaker from Lange and a watchmaker from Niton open together a watch signed Glashütte / Genf, fitted a century ago with a Niton calibre. In front of the collectors, they read it aloud: the calibre and its finishing, then what each recognises of his own craft.
s09.p2: The Niton name has been revived in Geneva by a new team. Its presence brings back the signature that equipped the branch's first watches.
s09.p3: Around the workbench, a display case gathers watches from the Geneva period, lent by the house, by collectors or by Geneva auction houses. A Cabaret accompanies them, the rectangular watch that since 1997 has continued the line of the shaped watches of the time.
s09.cabaretAlt: Rectangular Cabaret watch in pink gold, set bezel, mother-of-pearl dial with outsize date.
s09.oldCaption: Rectangular watch signed A. Lange & Söhne Genf, 1930s · glashuetteuhren.de
s09.oldAlt: Rectangular rose-gold wristwatch, silvered dial signed A. Lange & Söhne Genf, leather strap.
s09.calCaption: Calibre L931.3 of the Cabaret, seen from the caseback
s09.calAlt: The Cabaret's calibre L931.3 seen from the caseback: three-quarter plate with Glashütte stripes, gold chatons with blued screws, engraved balance cock, drawn to the scale of the watch.

s10.label: 21 · The Exchange of Discovery
s10.p1: A first encounter with the house, by hand. In the workshop, the watchmaker sets two movements side by side: a Geneva calibre from the 1920s and a Lange calibre of today, with its three-quarter plate in German silver, the signature of Glashütte.
s10.p2: The visitor learns to tell them apart with the loupe, then tries a watchmaker's gesture on a practice movement. They leave with an invitation to come back and discover the collections at a private appointment.
s10.caption: Lange movement, seen close · A. Lange & Söhne
s10.alt: Close-up of a Lange movement: bridges, rubies set in gold chatons, wheels and blued screws.

s11.label: 22 · The Exchange of Experiences
s11.p1: Clients come in groups of eight to ten, throughout the day. Each visit lasts about forty minutes and follows the thread of the story: the 1927 display case on the ground floor, a short film in the first-floor cinema, then the workshop, where the watchmaker shows his work on a movement in progress.
s11.p2: The visit ends in the salon over a glass of Geneva wine, with an adviser from the house, while the next group goes up to the workshop.
stops: A short film in the cinema
The salon, a glass of Geneva wine

s12.label: 23 · The Exchange of Taste
s12.p1: The dinner takes place in the boutique, around a single table of a few covers. It is repeated two or three evenings in a row, so that each guest stays within a very small circle.
s12.p2: In front of each guest lies a Lange watch, old or recent. Through the dinner, the watches pass from hand to hand and the conversation follows them round the table. A master watchmaker presents each piece and tells, from it, what Glashütte and Geneva have passed on to each other.
s12.p3: The menu blends the cuisines of the two cities, prepared four-handed by a Geneva chef and a Saxon chef.

a2.label: A6 · The Geneva watches, 1927-1936
a2.title: The Geneva watches, 1927-1936
a2.p1: The branch's first watches use a Niton shaped calibre of 9 × 11 lignes, engraved “A. Lange & Söhne, Geneva-Swiss, Eighteen Jewels, all Adjustments”, decorated with Geneva stripes and struck with two Geneva Seals. The same calibre equipped Patek Philippe watches at the time [3].
a2.p2a: No. 100009 has an octagonal tonneau case in green gold, 25 × 37 mm, set off with black enamel.
a2.p2c: It remained in the same family until 2009 [3].
a2.p3: From no. 100016, the branch sources from Altus, then adopts in 1931 an Altus shaped calibre of 8 ¼ × 12 lignes [3][11][12]. The watches, rectangular or tonneau, are sold under the names Lange-Uhr Glashütte and A. Lange & Söhne Genf [12].
a2.p4: The Cabaret, launched in 1997 with the L931 shaped calibre, continues this line. The Cabaret Tourbillon, born in 2008, had a Handwerkskunst edition of 30 pieces in 2021 and a Honeygold edition in 2026 [11][12].

a2b.reading: One line in an archive is enough to find a watch again: its number, its buyer, its price and its link with Geneva.

a1.label: A1 · Lange and Geneva, milestones
a1.title: Lange and Geneva, milestones
rows: Ferdinand Adolph Lange founds his manufacture in Glashütte.

The Niton manufacture is founded in Geneva by three watchmakers, two of them formerly of Vacheron Constantin. From 1921 to 1929, it ranks first or second for the number of movements certified with the Geneva Seal.
Lange's branch is entered in the Geneva commercial register, 25 Avenue du Mail, Plainpalais. Published on 6 May 1927.
First Geneva wristwatches, nos. 100008 to 100015, fitted with Niton calibres. Altus movements from no. 100016.

The first collection of the new era is presented at Dresden Castle.

e2.label: 01 · A house born of exchange
e2.p1: From 1837 to 1841, Ferdinand Adolph Lange trains in the great centres of precision watchmaking: near Paris with Joseph Thaddäus Winnerl, a pupil of Breguet, then in Switzerland and London. He brings back the metric system and the plan for a Saxon manufacture, which he founds in Glashütte in 1845.
e2.p2: In 1927, his grandsons make the same journey. The knowledge they lack, the wristwatch, is in Geneva.
e2.p3: In 2027, the house returns to Geneva with its own.
e2.quote: “Don't forget your home! It will welcome you back with open arms if you come back one day, rich in experience.”
e2.quoteBy: Gutkaes, in his apprentice's travelling book · A. Lange & Söhne [5]
e2.reading: Lange was founded on an exchange: seek out the best knowledge in Europe and transform it in Glashütte. It has been its method from the start.

route.alt: Schematic map of Europe: the founder's journey from Dresden to Paris, Switzerland and London from 1837 to 1841, then Glashütte in 1845.

e3.label: 02 · Receiving and giving
e3.a: Richard Lange, the founder's son, is 84. He reads an article by two Siemens engineers and turns it into a patent: a beryllium alloy for balance springs.
e3.b: The invention is taken up in Switzerland under the name Nivarox. This balance spring is used today in most quality mechanical watches.
e3.c: Walter Lange re-founds the house in Glashütte with Günter Blümlein, who came from Swiss watchmaking: Saxon knowledge and Swiss experience meet.
e3.reading: At Lange, exchange runs both ways: the house receives, transforms, and gives back to all of watchmaking. An exchange between equals.
e3.sources: A. Lange & Söhne, “Richard and Emil Lange” [17], “A. Lange & Söhne is reborn” [18].

e4.label: 04 · The foundations
items: Since 1837, the house has sought out the best knowledge wherever it is, and transformed it in Glashütte.
It receives and it gives: what it learns in turn feeds all of watchmaking.
Every boutique enters into dialogue with its city and its crafts.
e4.coda: For Geneva, the question becomes: what story does the house share with this city?

m1.label: 07 · 25, Avenue du Mail
m1.p1: The branch is the work of the third generation: Adolf-Otto, Wilhelm-Rudolf and Hans-Gerhard Lange, the founder's grandsons. They entrust its management to a man from Neuchâtel living in Petit-Saconnex, Paul Piaget, originally from Les Bayards.
m1.p2: Glashütte's management explains the choice of Geneva, “centre of the Swiss watch industry”, by the city's know-how in wristwatches. Manufacture and sales now take place in Switzerland, in Swiss francs.
m1.coda: Glashütte comes to Geneva to learn.
m1.alt: Line elevation of the building at 25, Avenue du Mail: four storeys and an attic above an arcaded ground floor, wrought-iron balconies.
m1.sources: Swiss Official Gazette of Commerce [1]; Deutsche Uhrmacher-Zeitung, 1927 [21]; Stegemann [3]; glashuetteuhren.de [4].

m2.label: 08 · Niton
m2.p1: For its first wristwatches, Lange turns to one of the finest manufactures in Geneva, founded in 1919: Niton.
m2.p2: In 1922, it ranks first in the Geneva official inspection; in 1928, it wins a prize at the Geneva chronometry competition. It supplies Cartier, Gübelin and Patek Philippe.
m2.p3: The branch's first watches receive its shaped calibres.
m2.captionA: The founders of Niton · Klassik Uhren 1/2019
m2.altA: Old photograph of three men in suits, the founders of the Niton manufacture, one holding a watch.
m2.altB: Niton advertisement of 1928: three rectangular dial models.

m3.label: 09 · Glashütte / Genf
m3.p1: The branch's watches bear both cities. On the first ones, the Niton movement is engraved “A. Lange & Söhne, Geneva-Swiss, Eighteen Jewels, all Adjustments” and decorated with Geneva stripes.
m3.p2: It is struck with two Geneva Seals, the hallmark the city reserves for its most carefully finished movements.
m3.p3a: The movements bear the words “Glashütte & Genf”, the dials “A. Lange & Söhne Genf”.
m3.dialAlt: Tonneau dial signed A. Lange & Söhne Genf, Arabic numerals, small seconds at six.

m4.label: 10 · The dispatch ledgers
m4.p1: The dispatch ledgers of the Geneva production are kept at the Deutsches Uhrenmuseum in Glashütte. They record 24 watches sold in 1927, 147 in 1928, about 150 in 1929, 49 in 1930 and 116 in 1931, shipped as far as Tokyo.
m4.p2: On 27 April 1929, no. 100118, a green gold watch with a Peseux calibre, goes to Eduard Riemer in Prague for 360 Swiss francs.

m5.label: 11 · 11 March 1936
m5.p1: Nine years after its entry, the branch is struck off the Geneva commercial register “following its closure”. The Official Gazette publishes it on 16 March 1936.
m5.p2: The house goes on selling wristwatches from Glashütte. Then the war, the expropriation of 1948 and forty years of interruption erase the memory of Geneva.
m5.coda: For almost a century, the story is forgotten.

af.label: A2 · Four generations
af.title: Four generations, one journey
af.intro: Generation after generation, the house goes elsewhere to find what it lacks, and brings it back to Glashütte.
head: Generation
Who
What they went to find elsewhere
rows: Paris, Switzerland and London, 1837 to 1841: the precision craft, the metric system and the idea of a manufacture.
Paris, where Emil sits on the World Fair jury; materials science, from which Richard's 1930 patent on the beryllium balance spring is born.
Geneva, 1927 to 1936: the wristwatch, with Niton and the Geneva suppliers.
The watchmaking school of Karlstein, in Austria, from 1941; in 1990, the re-founding with Günter Blümlein.
Geneva again: the Salon in 2021, the boutique on Rue Robert-Céard in 2027.

a.text: “Watches and supplies. — 3 May. The general partnership ‘A. Lange & Söhne Deutsche Uhrenfabrikation-Glashütte, in Glashütte (Saxony)’ (entered in the commercial register of Lauenstein [Saxony], per certificate issued on 30 March 1927), has established in Plainpalais a branch under the business name: A. Lange & Söhne Deutsche Uhrenfabrikation-Glashütte, in Glashütte, Geneva branch. This branch is represented by any one of the partners, who are: Adolf-Otto Lange; Wilhelm-Rudolf Lange and Hans-Gerhard Lange, all three of German nationality, residing in Glashütte, or by Paul Piaget, of Les Bayards (Neuchâtel), in Petit-Saconnex, manager of the branch, who has been granted power of attorney to this effect. an.label: A4 · Niton, 1919-1972
an.title: Niton, the forgotten manufacture
an.intro: The branch's Geneva supplier, after Sander Peeters's study.
rows: Founding of “Jeannet, Morel et Bourquin”, Rue du Mont-Blanc. Morel and Bourquin come from Vacheron Constantin (1908-1916).
The firm becomes the Manufacture des Montres Niton. First place in the Geneva official inspection ranking.
Niton supplies the first watches of the Lange branch, cases 100008 to 100015.
Prize at the Geneva chronometry competition, with calibre no. 4903.
Branch in New York, 607 Fifth Avenue.
Alfred Bourquin, left on his own, retires.
Part of the production rights sold to Ebauches SA; Niton makes movements for Chopard, Rolex and Universal until 1955.
Bought by Sarcar on 4 February 1957, then merged.
The name is relaunched in Geneva by a new team, with no corporate continuity.

ap.label: A5 · The Geneva Seal
ap.title: The Geneva Seal
ap.p1: Established by a Geneva law of 1886, the Geneva Seal distinguishes movements made, assembled and regulated in the canton, inspected against finishing criteria set by the State.
ap.p2: In the 1920s, Niton is among the manufactures submitting the most movements for inspection: from 1921 to 1929, it ranks first or second.
ap.p3: The Niton calibres of the branch's first watches bear two.
ap.caption: Niton shaped calibre, movement no. 4763 · after Stegemann

aq.label: A9 · Sensitive questions
aq.title: The questions the press will ask
aq.intro: Prepared answers, to be approved by the Maison. They are not on screen during the event.
rows: Did Lange sell Swiss watches under its name?
Yes, from 1927 to 1936, and openly: the watches bear “Genf” or “Geneva-Swiss”. In December 1928, the house even asked its retailers to say they did not have the precision of its pocket watches.
Didn't Lange sue those who combined Swiss movements with the Glashütte name?
Yes, in 1904, against the Union Horlogère. Twenty years later, the pocket-watch crisis forced the house to change strategy; it did so under a separate name, that of its Geneva branch.
Why did the branch close in 1936?
The sources consulted do not say. The house was then coming out of the crisis through public orders, in Glashütte.
Is Paul Piaget, the manager, related to the Piaget house?
No source consulted says so. Do not suggest it.

e5.label: 03 · Every boutique speaks its city
e5.p1: Lisbon, June 2026. On Avenida da Liberdade, the new boutique's reception is paved with calçada portuguesa, hand-laid in a fan pattern: the house sees in it an echo of the perlage on its plates.
e5.p2: London, December 2025. On Old Bond Street, the lounge takes up the spirit of the Mayfair clubs, and the house recalls its “historical ties” with the city, where its founder trained.
e5.reading: A Lange boutique is not a standard showcase: it takes root in its city and sets a local craft in dialogue with Glashütte's.
